titleEn: Six-Year-Old Bicycle Crash - Head Injury With Forearm Fracture

patient.name: Ethan Morris
patient.affectEn: six-year-old boy, crying and frightened, sitting in his mother's lap holding his left forearm against his chest; calms if you talk to him gently, get down to his level and let his mum hold his hand; asks 'where is my bike?' three times in two minutes (repetitive questioning) and has not been himself since the crash
patient.speechEn: single words or very short phrases ('my arm hurts'); his mother answers most of the history; he will not rate the pain with a number but will point to a faces scale; says his neck does not hurt but cannot stop crying about his arm

scene.settingEn: Quiet residential cul-de-sac off Hammond Bay Road in Nanaimo at 1615 hrs. Dry pavement, overcast, 14 degrees C, no traffic - a neighbour has parked across the entrance. A bicycle lies on its side at the bottom of a sloped driveway with the front wheel buckled. The boy is sitting on the grass beside the driveway in his mother's lap; his helmet is off, sitting beside him, with a visible crack across the left side. One patient. Fire first responders are 4 minutes out; Nanaimo Regional General Hospital is 10 minutes away.
hazardsEn: neighbour's vehicle parked across the cul-de-sac entrance to block traffic
the bicycle lying on its side at the bottom of the driveway

bystanders.knowsEn: Saw the whole thing. He was riding down the sloped driveway, the front wheel hit the lip of the gutter, and he went over the handlebars at low speed and landed on his left side with his head hitting the pavement, at about 1610 hrs. His helmet was on and is cracked on the left. He was limp and unresponsive for 'about five or ten seconds' and then started crying. He vomited once about five minutes later. No shaking or seizure. He keeps asking the same question about his bike and has not been himself since. Born at term, healthy, immunizations up to date, no previous head injury. No medications - she has not given him anything. No known allergies. Last ate a snack of crackers and juice at about 1530. He was 20 kg at his last check-up. She is tearful but cooperative, holds his hand, and gives consent for assessment and treatment when asked. At first she asks to drive him to hospital herself because he hates ambulances; if the need for spinal precautions and monitoring is explained calmly and she is offered a seat in the ambulance, she agrees to ride with him.
Parked across the entrance of the cul-de-sac to stop traffic. Did not see the crash. Will move the car or carry equipment if asked.
Dispatched with you, 4 minutes out at the time of the call. On arrival they can take over manual stabilization of the head or fetch equipment, but only on your direction.

scene.partnerEn: one partner at your licence level; acts only on your delegation
equipmentEn: pediatric hard collars (several sizes), towel rolls, foam head blocks and padding
pediatric spinal immobilization device with straps
forearm splints, roller bandages, sling and pillow for elevation
oxygen kit with pediatric masks and nasal cannula
pediatric and adult BP cuffs and stethoscope
length-based tape and pediatric drug reference
PCP only: IV start kit, ondansetron (oral), dimenhydrinate

dispatchEn: 1615 hrs. Code 3 to a residential cul-de-sac off Hammond Bay Road in Nanaimo. A six-year-old boy has come off his bicycle and struck his head. His mother is with him and called 911. Dry, overcast, 14 degrees C. Fire first responders are 4 minutes out. Nanaimo Regional General Hospital is 10 minutes away.
dispatchUpdateEn: Dispatch adds: the mother saw the whole thing. The boy went over the handlebars at low speed on a driveway slope, was wearing a helmet, and was 'out for a few seconds'. He is awake now, crying, and has vomited once. His left forearm looks bent.
arrivalEn: You pull into a quiet residential cul-de-sac; a neighbour has parked across the entrance to block traffic. Dry pavement, overcast, 14 degrees. A bicycle lies on its side at the bottom of a sloped driveway with its front wheel buckled. A young boy is sitting on the grass beside the driveway in his mother's lap. A helmet with a visible crack across the left side sits on the grass beside them. The mother is holding him, tearful but cooperative. She looks up at you: "Can I just drive him myself? He hates ambulances." One patient. No other hazards.
firstLookEn: A small boy of about six, awake and crying in his mother's lap, holding his left forearm against his chest. The forearm has an obvious deformity. No active bleeding anywhere. A cracked bicycle helmet lies on the grass beside him.

primary.locEn: Alert (AVPU = A). Crying, but looks at you and answers simple questions with single words; GCS 15 now. He asks 'where is my bike?' again and again - three times in two minutes (repetitive questioning). Dispatch and his mother report he was 'out' for a few seconds after the crash.
primary.airwayEn: Open and clear. He is crying loudly with no stridor; no blood, vomit or debris in the mouth.
primary.breathingEn: Respirations 24, unlaboured, regular, good bilateral air entry, equal chest rise. No accessory muscle use.
primary.circulationEn: Radial pulse 110, strong and regular. Capillary refill under 2 seconds. No external bleeding.
primary.rbsEn: HEAD: 3 cm boggy hematoma over the left parietal scalp, no depression, no bleeding. NECK: he says his neck does not hurt, but he cannot stop crying about his arm. Chest, abdomen and pelvis unremarkable. LEFT FOREARM: obvious closed mid-shaft deformity, skin intact; radial pulse strong, capillary refill normal, he can move his fingers and feels you touch them. Legs: a minor graze on the left knee only. No other injuries. Skin is given automatically during the RBS: warm, dry and pink, capillary refill under 2 seconds. SpO2 98% on room air if checked. (Examiner note, never volunteer: obvious injury above the clavicles, a witnessed loss of consciousness and a painful distracting forearm fracture mean NEXUS cannot clear his neck - spinal motion restriction is indicated.)
primary.skinEn: warm, dry and pink; capillary refill under 2 seconds

history.ccEn: (Child, crying, pointing to his left forearm:) "My arm hurts." (Mother:) "He came off his bike and hit his head on the pavement. He was out for a few seconds."

opqrst.oEn: (Mother:) "He was riding down our sloped driveway, the front wheel hit the lip of the gutter and he went over the handlebars. He wasn't going fast. He landed on his left side and his head hit the pavement - about ten past four. His helmet was on; it's cracked on the left side. He was limp and didn't respond for about five or ten seconds, then he started crying. He threw up once about five minutes later. No shaking, no seizure. He keeps asking me the same thing about his bike and he hasn't been himself since."
opqrst.pEn: He cries whenever the arm is moved; he is holding it still against his chest. Nothing has been given for it.
opqrst.qEn: He cannot describe it - he just says "it hurts" and cries.
opqrst.rEn: (Child points to the middle of his left forearm.) The pain stays in the arm. (Only if asked directly about his head:) "My head hurts."
opqrst.sEn: He will not give a number. Shown a faces scale, he points to the second-worst face.
opqrst.tEn: (Mother:) "It happened at about ten past four, just before I called. It's hurt since he landed on it."

history.painScoreEn: No number - on a faces scale he picks the second-worst face (after splinting and cold he picks the middle face).

sample.sEn: Left forearm pain, the bump on his head, one vomit about five minutes after the crash, and he keeps asking the same question. (Only if asked:) his head hurts and the lights are too bright.
sample.mEn: (Mother:) "He doesn't take any medicine. I haven't given him anything for this."
sample.pEn: (Mother:) "He's healthy. He was born on time, his shots are all up to date, and he's never had a head injury before." (Only if asked his weight:) "He was 20 kilos at his last check-up."
sample.lEn: (Mother:) "A snack of crackers and juice at about half past three (1530)."
sample.eEn: (Mother:) "He was riding his bike down our driveway. The front wheel caught the lip of the gutter and he went straight over the handlebars."

fe.generalEn: (Mother:) "He's normally a healthy, active boy. He's been eating and drinking well, no recent illness."
fe.cnsEn: He was knocked out briefly and keeps asking the same question. (Child, when asked:) "My head hurts." No seizure, no weakness, no numbness.
fe.giGuEn: He threw up once, about five minutes after the crash, and not since. No tummy pain. He passed urine normally this afternoon.
fe.integumentaryEn: The bump on his head and a graze on his left knee. No other cuts, bruises or rashes.
fe.eentEn: No bleeding or fluid from the nose or ears. (Mother:) "His eyes look normal to me." (Child:) "The lights are too bright."

findings.headNeckEn: 3 cm boggy hematoma over the left parietal scalp, no depression. No bruising behind the ears; no blood or fluid from the ears or nose. No midline cervical tenderness - but he is distracted by his arm, so this does not clear his neck.
findings.chestLungsEn: No tenderness or deformity. Equal air entry, clear in all 6 sites. No seat-belt or handlebar mark.
findings.abdomenEn: Soft and non-tender in all four quadrants. Specifically, NO handlebar bruise over the epigastrium.
findings.backEn: No tenderness, no deformity (checked when he is moved onto the device).
findings.lowerExtremitiesEn: Grazed left knee, otherwise normal. Normal circulation, sensation and movement in both feet.
findings.upperExtremitiesEn: LEFT FOREARM: obvious closed mid-shaft deformity, skin intact. Distal radial pulse strong, capillary refill under 2 seconds, he can wiggle his fingers and feels you touch them - before and after splinting. RIGHT ARM: normal, no injury - the arm for the BP cuff and SpO2 probe.

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: baseline, on scene (pediatric cuff, uninjured right arm); all values normal for a six-year-old
vitalsSets.skin: warm, dry and pink; capillary refill under 2 seconds

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: in the ambulance, about 15 minutes after set 1, after splinting and cold; calmer, has not vomited again, no longer asking the repeated question; faces-scale pain down to the middle face
vitalsSets.skin: warm, dry and pink; capillary refill under 2 seconds

stateChanges.examinerLineEn: The mother asks again, more insistently: "Can I just drive him myself? He hates ambulances."
He pushes the mouthpiece away and cries harder; he cannot make a seal or follow your breathing instructions.

expected.actionEn: Acknowledge and plan pediatric equipment: pediatric collar or a towel-roll and blocks if no collar fits, padding to keep a small child neutral, arm splints, a length-based tape or weight estimate, and the pediatric drug reference
Plan the approach to the family as well as the patient: a calm parent is your best assessment tool and an upset parent is your biggest obstacle

Verbalize hazards (driveway slope, the neighbour's vehicle blocking traffic, the bicycle), environment, MOI (over the handlebars at low speed, helmet struck and cracked on the left) and people (one child plus one parent)
Don gloves; get down to the child's level, speak to him before you speak about him, and ask the mother's permission to examine him - she gives consent for treatment
First look: alert crying child, holding his left forearm against his chest, an obvious deformity, no active bleeding, and a cracked helmet as direct evidence that the head took the impact
Assess LOC / AVPU: alert, GCS 15 now, but document the witnessed loss of consciousness and the repetitive questioning as evidence of a brain injury even though he looks well
triggers: do you know where you are

expected.actionEn: Apply spinal motion restriction: he has an obvious injury above the level of the clavicles, a witnessed LOC and a painful distracting forearm fracture, so his neck cannot be cleared by NEXUS no matter what he says about it
Assess the airway; a strong loud cry is a reassuring airway sign in a child
triggers: crying so his airway is open

expected.actionEn: Assess breathing and interpret the rate against pediatric norms - 24 is normal for a six-year-old, whereas the same rate in an adult would be abnormal
triggers: breathing is normal for his age

expected.actionEn: Assess circulation with a radial pulse and capillary refill; know that children compensate for shock by raising the heart rate and hold their blood pressure until they crash suddenly
Rapid body survey head to toe, explaining each step to the child in words he understands and examining the painful arm last
Note the skin as warm, dry and pink with capillary refill under 2 seconds
Oxygen: keep SpO2 at or above 94% for any head injury - at 98% on room air supplemental oxygen is not required, and say so rather than applying it out of habit
triggers: keep his sats at or above 94

expected.actionEn: Position: keep him with his mother, immobilized but comfortable, and elevate the head of the device 30 degrees for the head injury once he is secured
triggers: head of the board up 30 degrees

expected.actionEn: Correctly categorize as non-RTC with the reasons stated: GCS 15, stable vitals, patent airway, no unstable criteria met
State the upgrade triggers: any fall in GCS, repeated vomiting, changing heart rate, unequal pupils or a seizure makes this RTC
Manage the parent: explain the need for ambulance transport in plain language, obtain consent, keep her with the child, and do not let the child leave by private vehicle
triggers: ride with us in the ambulance
he needs to go by ambulance
keep his neck still on the way

expected.actionEn: Establish the chief complaint: left forearm pain and a head injury with a witnessed brief loss of consciousness

HxC/C from the parent covering the fall questions and the head injury specifics: height and speed, what he struck, what hit first, helmet worn and damaged, exact duration of the LOC, number of vomits, seizure activity, and any change in behaviour since
triggers: how many times did he vomit

expected.actionEn: Pain score using an age-appropriate tool such as a faces scale rather than asking a six-year-old for a number
Past medical history including birth history and immunizations
Medications, including anything given by the parent before your arrival
triggers: anything for the pain before we got here

expected.actionEn: Allergies
Last oral intake and an accurate weight - both drive pediatric drug dosing and anaesthetic planning
GCS with all three components, using age-appropriate expectations for the verbal score
Blood pressure with a correctly sized pediatric cuff on the uninjured arm, interpreted against pediatric norms
Pulse rate, rhythm and quality, interpreted against pediatric norms - and remember bradycardia in a head-injured child is a late and ominous sign
Respiratory rate, depth and character against pediatric norms
Skin assessed hands-on with capillary refill, which is more useful than blood pressure in a child
Pupils - the single most important repeated observation in a head-injured child
SpO2, targeting 94% or above for the head injury
Blood glucose - indicated by the reported loss of consciousness
Temperature
FE - General health
FE - CNS (headache, photophobia and repetitive questioning are the concussion cluster)
FE - Respiratory
FE - Cardiovascular
FE - GI/GU (the number of vomits matters in a head injury)
FE - Integumentary
FE - Musculoskeletal
FE - Endocrine
FE - EENT (photophobia, and checking ears and nose for blood or fluid)
Head and neck examined including behind the ears and the ear canals, before the collar is applied
Chest examined with six-site auscultation and inspected for a handlebar mark
Abdomen examined specifically for handlebar injury - a classic and easily missed pediatric bicycle injury
Back examined during the transfer onto the device
Upper extremities with CSM above and below the deformity documented before and after splinting
Lower extremities with CSM
Pediatric spinal immobilization done correctly: neutral position with padding UNDER THE SHOULDERS, correctly sized collar or manual stabilization with towel rolls, body secured, head never taped
triggers: secure his body to the board

expected.actionEn: Splint the left forearm in the position found, immobilizing the joints above and below, with CSM checked and documented before and after, plus cold and elevation
triggers: splint it in the position found
elevate the arm on a pillow

expected.actionEn: Head injury management: SpO2 kept at or above 94%, head of the device elevated 30 degrees, the collar kept loose, and GCS and pupils reassessed every 5 minutes
triggers: SpO2 at or above 94 for the head injury

expected.actionEn: If analgesia is given, use weight-based ibuprofen 10 mg/kg PO - 200 mg for a 20 kg child - and never an adult dose; state the weight you used and how you obtained it
Rule out and verbalize the pediatric analgesia restrictions: methoxyflurane is contraindicated under 18, and Entonox requires self-administration and cooperation this child cannot reliably give
Family-centred care: keep the mother with the child throughout, explain each step in words the child understands, obtain parental consent, and refuse the private-vehicle transport politely but firmly
triggers: I'm going to explain what we're doing
is that okay with you mom

expected.actionEn: Reassess ABCs and interventions after every move and at least every 5 minutes
Serial GCS and pupil checks documented with times - the trend is what the receiving team needs
Second full set of vitals within 15 minutes for a non-priority patient
Recheck CSM distal to the forearm splint after every move and re-score the pain with the faces scale
Keep suction ready in case he vomits again while immobilized, and be ready to tip the whole device
triggers: turn the board on its side

expected.actionEn: Notification appropriate to a stable pediatric head injury
Complete hand-off with the LOC duration, vomit count, serial GCS and pupils, and the exact ibuprofen dose in mg/kg if given
Accurate PCR within 5 minutes, documenting the weight used for dosing and the parental consent

specialEvents.descriptionEn: after spinal motion restriction is started, the candidate lets go of manual stabilization of the head before the collar, blocks and body straps are all in place, or lets the child sit up, turn his head freely, stand, walk, or be picked up and carried by his mother. Handing manual stabilization over to the partner, a first responder or the mother (with instructions) is NOT a release.
candidate pads under the child's shoulders / upper back (towel, blanket or padding) so his proportionally large head does not flex his neck forward on the device
candidate tapes the child's head to the spinal device (e.g. tape across the forehead or chin)
candidate actually gives Entonox to the child (hands him the mouthpiece or tells him to breathe it). Saying that Entonox cannot be used is NOT this event. Also log drug:entonox.
candidate actually gives methoxyflurane (Penthrox) to the child. Saying it is contraindicated is NOT this event. Also log drug:methoxyflurane.
candidate actually gives acetaminophen (Tylenol) to the child at any dose. Asking the mother whether she gave him any, or saying it will not be given, is NOT this event. Also log drug:acetaminophen.

candidate actually gives the child ibuprofen now. Record it at the moment it is given (also log drug:ibuprofen) - never for a question to the mother about whether he had any, never for a plan, and never for a dose calculation.
ibuprofen given at a dose other than 10 mg/kg (200 mg for his 20 kg) - for example an adult 300-400 mg dose - or by a route other than by mouth, or a second dose given during this call

candidate agrees that the mother may take the child to hospital in her own car, or leaves him at the scene, instead of ambulance transport. Refusing her request, or offering her a seat in the ambulance, is NOT this event.
candidate sends the mother away from the child, refuses to let her stay beside him, or refuses to let her ride in the ambulance
candidate explains to the mother why the child needs the ambulance (spinal precautions, monitoring) and/or offers her a seat in the ambulance

candidate splints the left forearm without checking distal circulation, sensation and movement (radial pulse or capillary refill, finger movement and sensation) first, or does not recheck them after the splint is on
the forearm splint does not immobilize both the wrist and the elbow (the joints above and below the fracture)
candidate puts the BP cuff (or inflates a cuff) on the injured left arm
candidate takes the BP with an adult cuff on this child without verbalizing the cuff size or correcting it
candidate gives TXA (tranexamic acid). Saying TXA is contraindicated in an isolated head injury is NOT this event. Also log drug:txa.
candidate gives ondansetron or dimenhydrinate (also log drug:ondansetron or drug:dimenhydrinate)
PCP gives dimenhydrinate to this 20 kg child without first contacting the ER (the monograph says contact ER if the patient appears to be under 25 kg)
PCP gives ondansetron at a dose other than 4 mg by mouth (the BC pediatric dose for 4 years and older), or by another route

drugs.doseEn: 10 mg/kg PO - 200 mg for this 20 kg child (weight from his mother: 20 kg at his last check-up); may repeat once after 6 hours; maximum 40 mg/kg/day. Only after baseline vitals, and only if he is fully alert and has not vomited again; state the weight used and how it was obtained.
drugs.contraindicationsEn: hypersensitivity to ibuprofen or other NSAIDs; active GI hemorrhage or ulcers; pregnancy; anticoagulants
drugs.cautionsEn: history of gastrointestinal, renal or significant cardiovascular disease

drugs.doseEn: NOT GIVEN in this scenario: the BC monograph lists adult dosing only (500-1,000 mg PO) and has no pediatric dose, so any dose to this 20 kg child is outside the protocol (if given, report drug:acetaminophen and acetaminophen-given)

WITHHELD: inhalation, self-administered only. A distressed six-year-old cannot reliably self-administer or comply (contraindication: inability to comply), and altered level of consciousness is also a contraindication (if given, report drug:entonox and entonox-given-to-child)
drugs.contraindicationsEn: inability to comply; inability to ventilate an enclosed treatment area; decompression sickness; altered level of consciousness; pneumothorax; air embolism; inhalation injury; nitroglycerin used in the last 5 minutes

drugs.doseEn: WITHHELD: contraindicated in patients less than 18 years of age and in decreased level of consciousness or head injury (adult dose 3 mL self-administered via inhaler; if given, report drug:methoxyflurane and methoxyflurane-given)
PCP only: 4 mg PO (BC pediatric dose for 4 years and older), only if he vomits again or has moderate to severe nausea; not EMR scope
drugs.contraindicationsEn: known allergy or hypersensitivity to ondansetron; congenital long QT syndrome; phenylketonuria (ODT form)

drugs.doseEn: PCP only: 1 mg/kg to a maximum of 50 mg IM or IV - the monograph says contact ER if the patient appears to be under 25 kg (he is 20 kg); not EMR scope
NOT INDICATED: TXA is contraindicated for isolated traumatic brain injury and in patients under 12 years, and there is no hemorrhagic shock; not EMR scope (if given, report drug:txa and txa-given)

examinerPrompts.missedInjuryEn: You did a rapid body survey - what did you find on his head and on his arms?

trackNotes.emrEn: Everything this child needs is EMR scope: spinal motion restriction in a neutral position with padding under the shoulders, a correctly sized pediatric collar (or towel rolls and blocks), head of the device elevated 30 degrees with the collar loose, SpO2 kept at or above 94%, a forearm splint with cold, elevation and CSM checks, suction ready, and serial GCS and pupil checks. The graded judgement is the analgesia decision: methoxyflurane is contraindicated under 18 and with a head injury, Entonox needs a cooperative self-administering patient, acetaminophen has no pediatric dose in the BC monograph, and the only weight-based option is ibuprofen 10 mg/kg PO - 200 mg for 20 kg - after baseline vitals. Non-drug analgesia and a parent at the bedside do most of the work. IV access, ondansetron, dimenhydrinate and TXA are outside EMR scope. No Functional Enquiry.
trackNotes.pcpEn: PCP adds the 9-system Functional Enquiry. For further vomiting PCP may give ondansetron 4 mg PO (the BC pediatric dose for 4 years and older); dimenhydrinate requires contacting the ER because he is under 25 kg. PCP keeps the blood glucose between 4.0 and 8.0 mmol/L per the TBI protocol and would consider vascular access if his LOC deteriorates. TXA is contraindicated (isolated traumatic brain injury, under 12 years). Everything else is identical.
